<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt2" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAw" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"redirect","href":"./Template:Redirect"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Lightning tree"},"2":{"wt":"the song \"The Lightning Tree\""},"3":{"wt":"Follyfoot"}},"i":0}}]}"><style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1368532237" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" about="#mwt3" data-mw="{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}">.mw-parser-output .hatnote{font-style:italic}.mw-parser-output div.hatnote{padding-left:1.6em;margin-bottom:0.5em}.mw-parser-output .hatnote i{font-style:normal}.mw-parser-output .hatnote+.mw-empty-elt+.hatnote{margin-top:-0.5em}@media print{body.ns-0 .mw-parser-output .hatnote{display:none!important}}</style></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt2" id="mwBA">"Lightning tree" redirects here. For the song "The Lightning Tree", see <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Follyfoot" title="Follyfoot">Follyfoot</a>.</div>

<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBQ"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PlanePair2.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwBg"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PlanePair2.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/PlanePair2.jpg/250px-PlanePair2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/PlanePair2.jpg/500px-PlanePair2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="951" data-file-height="864" data-file-type="bitmap" height="227" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwBw"></a><figcaption id="mwCA">Modern 3D Lichtenberg figures or "<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_treeing" title="Electrical treeing" id="mwCQ">electrical treeing</a>" in a block of clear acrylic, created by irradiating the block with an <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_beam" title="Electron beam" class="mw-redirect" id="mwCg">electron beam</a>. Actual size: <span about="#mwt4" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwCw" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"cvt","href":"./Template:Cvt"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"3"},"2":{"wt":"×"},"3":{"wt":"3"},"4":{"wt":"×"},"5":{"wt":"2"},"6":{"wt":"in"},"7":{"wt":"mm"},"order":{"wt":"flip"},"sigfig":{"wt":"1"}},"i":0}}]}">80</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt4"> </span><span about="#mwt4">mm ×</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt4"> </span><span about="#mwt4">80</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt4"> </span><span about="#mwt4">mm ×</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt4"> </span><span about="#mwt4">50</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt4"> </span><span about="#mwt4">mm (3</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt4"> </span><span about="#mwt4">in ×</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt4"> </span><span about="#mwt4">3</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt4"> </span><span about="#mwt4">in ×</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt4"> </span><span about="#mwt4">2</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt4"> </span><span about="#mwt4">in)</span></figcaption></figure>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwDA"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lichtenberg_figures_in_gases_generated_by_a_sliding_spark_discharge.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwDQ"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lichtenberg_figures_in_gases_generated_by_a_sliding_spark_discharge.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Lichtenberg_figures_in_gases_generated_by_a_sliding_spark_discharge.jpg/250px-Lichtenberg_figures_in_gases_generated_by_a_sliding_spark_discharge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Lichtenberg_figures_in_gases_generated_by_a_sliding_spark_discharge.jpg/500px-Lichtenberg_figures_in_gases_generated_by_a_sliding_spark_discharge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail 2x" alt="Lichtenberg figures are generated by a sliding spark discharge on the flask with a mixture of gases. Structural differences between the "positive" and "negative" figures can be observed." data-file-width="3840" data-file-height="2160" data-file-type="bitmap" height="124" width="220" class="mw-file-element" id="mwDg"></a><figcaption id="mwDw">Lichtenberg figures are generated by a sliding spark discharge on the flask with a mixture of gases. Structural differences between the "positive" and "negative" figures can be observed.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwEA"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lightning_injury.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwEQ"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lightning_injury.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/Lightning_injury.jpg/250px-Lightning_injury.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/Lightning_injury.jpg/500px-Lightning_injury.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="4320" data-file-height="3240" data-file-type="bitmap" height="188" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwEg"></a><figcaption id="mwEw">The slight branching redness traveling up this person's leg <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning_injury" title="Lightning injury" id="mwFA">was created</a> by current from a nearby <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning_strike" title="Lightning strike" id="mwFQ">lightning strike</a>.</figcaption></figure>

<p id="mwFg">A <b id="mwFw">Lichtenberg figure</b> (<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language" title="German language" about="#mwt5" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwGA" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"langx","href":"./Template:Langx"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"de"},"2":{"wt":"Lichtenberg-Figur"}},"i":0}}]}">German</a><span about="#mwt5">: </span><i lang="de" about="#mwt5">Lichtenberg-Figur</i><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_German-language_text" about="#mwt5" id="mwGQ">), or <b id="mwGg">Lichtenberg dust figure</b>, is a branching <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_discharge" title="Electric discharge" id="mwGw">electric discharge</a> that sometimes appears on the surface or in the interior of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_insulation" title="Electrical insulation" class="mw-redirect" id="mwHA">insulating materials</a>. Lichtenberg figures are often associated with the progressive deterioration of high-voltage components and equipment. The  study of planar Lichtenberg figures along insulating surfaces and 3D <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_treeing" title="Electrical treeing" id="mwHQ">electrical trees</a> within insulating materials often provides engineers with valuable insights for improving the long-term reliability of high-voltage equipment. Lichtenberg figures are now known to occur on or within solids, liquids, and gases during <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_breakdown" title="Electrical breakdown" id="mwHg">electrical breakdown</a>.</p>

<p id="mwHw">Lichtenberg figures are natural phenomena that exhibit <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractal" title="Fractal" id="mwIA">fractal</a> properties.</p>

<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" id="mwIQ" data-mw="{"autoGenerated":true}"></section><section data-mw-section-id="1" id="mwIg" aria-labelledby="History"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="History">History</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Lichtenberg_figure&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: History"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p id="mwIw">Lichtenberg figures are named after the German physicist <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Christoph_Lichtenberg" title="Georg Christoph Lichtenberg" id="mwJA">Georg Christoph Lichtenberg</a>, who originally discovered and studied them. When they were first discovered, it was thought that their characteristic shapes might help to reveal the nature of positive and negative electric "fluids".</p>

<p id="mwJQ">In 1777, Lichtenberg built a large <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrophorus" title="Electrophorus" id="mwJg">electrophorus</a> to generate high-<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltage" title="Voltage" id="mwJw">voltage</a> <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Static_electricity" title="Static electricity" id="mwKA">static electricity</a> through <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrostatic_induction" title="Electrostatic induction" id="mwKQ">induction</a>. After discharging a high-voltage point to the surface of an insulator, he recorded the resulting radial patterns by sprinkling various powdered materials onto the surface. By then pressing blank sheets of paper onto these patterns, Lichtenberg was able to transfer and record these images, thereby discovering the basic principle of modern <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xerography" title="Xerography" id="mwKg">xerography</a>.<sup about="#mwt6" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-1"}}"><a href="#cite_note-1" id="mwKw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwLA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwLQ">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwLg">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwLw">This discovery was also the forerunner of the modern day science of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_(physics)" title="Plasma (physics)" id="mwMA">plasma physics</a>. Although Lichtenberg only studied two-dimensional (2D) figures, modern high-voltage researchers study 2D and 3D figures (<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_tree" title="Electrical tree" class="mw-redirect" id="mwMQ">electrical trees</a>) on, and within, insulating materials.</p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="2" id="mwMg" aria-labelledby="Formation"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Formation">Formation</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Lichtenberg_figure&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Formation"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p id="mwMw">Two-dimensional (2D) Lichtenberg figures can be produced by placing a sharp-pointed needle perpendicular to the surface of a non-conducting plate, such as of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resin" title="Resin" id="mwNA">resin</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebonite" title="Ebonite" id="mwNQ">ebonite</a>, or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass" title="Glass" id="mwNg">glass</a>. The point is positioned very near or contacting the plate. A source of high voltage such as a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leyden_jar" title="Leyden jar" id="mwNw">Leyden jar</a> (an early type of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capacitor" title="Capacitor" id="mwOA">capacitor</a>) or a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Static_electricity" title="Static electricity" id="mwOQ">static electricity</a> generator is applied to the needle, typically through a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spark_gap" title="Spark gap" id="mwOg">spark gap</a>. This creates a sudden, small <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrostatic_discharge" title="Electrostatic discharge" id="mwOw">electrical discharge</a> along the surface of the plate. This deposits stranded areas of charge onto the surface of the plate. These electrified areas are then tested by sprinkling a mixture of powdered flowers of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur" title="Sulfur" id="mwPA">sulfur</a> and red lead (Pb<sub id="mwPQ">3</sub>O<sub id="mwPg">4</sub> or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_tetroxide" title="Lead tetroxide" class="mw-redirect" id="mwPw">lead tetroxide</a>) onto the plate.<sup about="#mwt9" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-2"}}"><a href="#cite_note-2" id="mwQA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwQQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwQg">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwQw">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwRA">Sulfur and red lead exhibit the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triboelectric_effect" title="Triboelectric effect" id="mwRQ">triboelectric effect</a>. During handling, powdered sulfur particles tend to acquire a negative charge. Similarly, powdered red lead particles tend to acquire a positive charge. The negatively-charged sulfur particles are electrostatically attracted and adhere to the positively electrified areas of the plate, while the positively charged red lead particles are attracted to the negatively electrified areas.</p>

<p id="mwRg">In addition to the distribution of colors thereby produced, there is also a marked difference in the form of the figure, according to the polarity of the electrical charge that was applied to the plate. If the charged areas were positive, a widely extending patch is seen on the plate, consisting of a dense nucleus from which branches radiate in all directions. Negatively charged areas are considerably smaller and have a sharp circular or fan-like boundary entirely devoid of branches. <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Rudolf_Hertz" title="Heinrich Rudolf Hertz" class="mw-redirect" id="mwRw">Heinrich Rudolf Hertz</a> employed Lichtenberg dust figures in his seminal work proving <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clerk_Maxwell" title="James Clerk Maxwell" id="mwSA">Maxwell's</a> electromagnetic wave theories.<sup about="#mwt12" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-3" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-3"}}"><a href="#cite_note-3" id="mwSQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwSg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwSw">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwTA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwTQ"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tracking1.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwTg"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tracking1.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Tracking1.jpg/250px-Tracking1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Tracking1.jpg/500px-Tracking1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="539" data-file-height="438" data-file-type="bitmap" height="203" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwTw"></a><figcaption id="mwUA">Carbonized high-voltage discharge tracks cross the surface of a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polycarbonate" title="Polycarbonate" id="mwUQ">polycarbonate</a> sheet.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwUg">If the plate receives a mixture of positive and negative charges as, for example, from an <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Induction_coil" title="Induction coil" id="mwUw">induction coil</a>, a mixed figure results, consisting of a large red central nucleus, corresponding to the negative charge, surrounded by yellow rays, corresponding to the positive charge. The difference between positive and negative figures seems to depend on the presence of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air" title="Air" class="mw-redirect" id="mwVA">air</a>, for the difference tends to disappear when the experiment is conducted in a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum" title="Vacuum" id="mwVQ">vacuum</a>. <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Theophil_Riess" title="Peter Theophil Riess" id="mwVg">Peter T. Riess</a> (a 19th-century researcher) theorized that the negative electrification of the plate was caused by the friction of the water vapour, etc., driven along the surface by the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explosion" title="Explosion" id="mwVw">explosion</a> that accompanies the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disruptive_discharge" title="Disruptive discharge" class="mw-redirect" id="mwWA">disruptive discharge</a> at the point. This electrification would favor the spread of a positive, but hinder that of a negative discharge.<sup about="#mwt15" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-4" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-4"}}"><a href="#cite_note-4" id="mwWQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwWg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwWw">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwXA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwXQ">It is now known that electrical charges are transferred to the insulator's surface through small spark discharges that occur along the boundary between the gas and insulator surface.<sup about="#mwt18" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-5" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-5"}}"><a href="#cite_note-5" id="mwXg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwXw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwYA">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwYQ">]</span></span></a></sup> Once transferred to the insulator, these excess charges become temporarily stranded. The shapes of the resulting charge distributions reflect the shape of the spark discharges which, in turn, depend on the high voltage polarity and pressure of the gas. Using a higher applied voltage will generate larger-diameter and more branched figures. It is now known that positive Lichtenberg figures have longer, branching structures because long sparks within air can more easily form and propagate from positively charged high-voltage terminals. This property has been used to measure the transient voltage polarity and magnitude of lightning surges on electrical power lines.<sup about="#mwt21" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-6" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-6"}}"><a href="#cite_note-6" id="mwYg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwYw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwZA">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwZQ">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwZg">Another type of 2D Lichtenberg figure can be created when an insulating surface becomes contaminated with semiconducting material. When a high voltage is applied across the surface, leakage currents may cause localized heating and progressive degradation and charring of the underlying material. Over time, branching, tree-like carbonized patterns are formed upon the surface of the insulator, called <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_tree" title="Electrical tree" class="mw-redirect" id="mwZw">electrical trees</a>. This degradation process is called <i id="mwaA">tracking</i>. If the conductive paths ultimately bridge the insulating space, the result is catastrophic failure of the insulating material. Some artists moisten the surface of wood or cardboard with a semiconductive <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolyte" title="Electrolyte" id="mwaQ">electrolytic</a> solution and then apply a high voltage across the surface to induce tracking, thereby creating complex carbonized 2D <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lichtenberg_figures" title="Lichtenberg figures" class="mw-redirect" id="mwag">Fractal burning</a> on the surface.</p>

<section data-mw-section-id="3" id="mwaw" aria-labelledby="Fractal_similarities"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Fractal_similarities">Fractal similarities</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Lichtenberg_figure&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Fractal similarities"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p id="mwbA">The branching, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-similar" title="Self-similar" class="mw-redirect" id="mwbQ">self-similar</a> patterns observed in Lichtenberg figures exhibit <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractal" title="Fractal" id="mwbg">fractal</a> properties. Lichtenberg figures often develop during the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dielectric_breakdown" title="Dielectric breakdown" class="mw-redirect" id="mwbw">dielectric breakdown</a> of solids, liquids, and even gases. Their appearance and growth appear to be related to a process called <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffusion-limited_aggregation" title="Diffusion-limited aggregation" id="mwcA">diffusion-limited aggregation</a> (DLA). A useful macroscopic model that combines an electric field with DLA was developed by Niemeyer, Pietronero, and Weismann in 1984, and is known as the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dielectric_breakdown_model" title="Dielectric breakdown model" id="mwcQ">dielectric breakdown model</a> (DBM).<sup about="#mwt24" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-7" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-7"}}"><a href="#cite_note-7" id="mwcg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwcw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwdA">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwdQ">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwdg">Although the electrical breakdown mechanisms of air and PMMA plastic are considerably different, the branching discharge structures turn out to be related. The branching forms taken by natural lightning also have fractal characteristics.<sup about="#mwt25" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-8" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-8"}}"><a href="#cite_note-8" id="mwdw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mweA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mweQ">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket" id="mweg">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="4" id="mwew" aria-labelledby="Constructal_law"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Constructal_law">Constructal law</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Lichtenberg_figure&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Constructal law"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p id="mwfA">Lichtenberg figures are examples of natural phenomena that exhibit <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractal" title="Fractal" id="mwfQ">fractal</a> properties. The emergence and evolution of these and the other tree-like structures that abound in nature are summarized by the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructal_law" title="Constructal law" class="mw-redirect" id="mwfg">constructal law</a>. First published by Duke professor <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Bejan" title="Adrian Bejan" id="mwfw">Adrian Bejan</a> in 1996, the constructal law is a first principle of physics that summarizes the tendency in nature to generate configurations (patterns, designs) that facilitate the free movement of the imposed currents that flow through it. The constructal law predicts that the tree-like designs described in this article should emerge and evolve to facilitate the movement (point-to-area) of the electrical currents flowing through them.<sup about="#mwt26" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-9" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-9"}}"><a href="#cite_note-9" id="mwgA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwgQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwgg">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwgw">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section></section><section data-mw-section-id="5" id="mwhA" aria-labelledby="Natural_occurrences"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Natural_occurrences">Natural occurrences</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Lichtenberg_figure&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Natural occurrences"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwhQ"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lightning_in_Arlington.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwhg"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lightning_in_Arlington.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Lightning_in_Arlington.jpg/250px-Lightning_in_Arlington.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Lightning_in_Arlington.jpg/500px-Lightning_in_Arlington.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="1327" data-file-height="1200" data-file-type="bitmap" height="226" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwhw"></a><figcaption id="mwiA"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning" title="Lightning" id="mwiQ">Lightning</a> is a naturally occurring three-dimensional Lichtenberg figure.</figcaption></figure>

<p id="mwig">Lichtenberg figures are fern-like patterns that may appear on the skin of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning_strike" title="Lightning strike" id="mwiw">lightning strike</a> victims and typically disappear in 24 hours.<sup about="#mwt30" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-10" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-10"}}"><a href="#cite_note-10" id="mwjA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwjQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwjg">[</span>10<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwjw">]</span></span></a></sup> They are also known as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keraunography" title="Keraunography" id="mwkA">Keraunographic markings</a>.<sup about="#mwt31" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-11" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-11"}}"><a href="#cite_note-11" id="mwkQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwkg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwkw">[</span>11<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwlA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwlQ">A lightning strike can also create a large Lichtenberg figure in grass surrounding the point struck. These are sometimes found on <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf_course" title="Golf course" id="mwlg">golf courses</a> or in grassy meadows.<sup about="#mwt32" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-12" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-12"}}"><a href="#cite_note-12" id="mwlw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwmA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwmQ">[</span>12<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwmg">]</span></span></a></sup>  Branching root-shaped "<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulgurite" title="Fulgurite" id="mwmw">fulgurite</a>" mineral deposits may also be created as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sand" title="Sand" id="mwnA">sand</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil" title="Soil" id="mwnQ">soil</a> are fused into glassy tubes by the intense ionizing electrical current, an effect  often seen in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_vapor_deposition" title="Chemical vapor deposition" id="mwng">chemical vapor deposition</a> when using <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc_discharge" title="Arc discharge" class="mw-redirect" id="mwnw">arc discharge</a> to produce <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesis_of_carbon_nanotubes#Arc_discharge" title="Synthesis of carbon nanotubes" id="mwoA">carbon nanotubes</a>.</p>

<p id="mwoQ"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_treeing" title="Electrical treeing" id="mwog">Electrical treeing</a> often occurs in high-voltage equipment prior to causing complete breakdown. Following these Lichtenberg figures within the insulation during post-accident investigation of an insulation failure can be useful in finding the cause of breakdown. From the direction and shape of the trees and their branches, an experienced high-voltage engineer can see exactly the point where the insulation began to break down, and using that knowledge, possibly find the initial cause as well. Broken-down transformers, high-voltage cables, bushings, and other equipment can usefully be investigated in this manner. The insulation is unrolled (in the case of paper insulation) or sliced in thin slices (in the case of solid insulating materials). The results are then sketched or photographed to create a record of the breakdown process.</p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="6" id="mwow" aria-labelledby="In_insulating_materials"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="In_insulating_materials">In insulating materials</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Lichtenberg_figure&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: In insulating materials"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p id="mwpA">Modern Lichtenberg figures can also be created within solid insulating materials, such as acrylic (polymethyl methacrylate, or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poly(methyl_methacrylate)" title="Poly(methyl methacrylate)" id="mwpQ">PMMA</a>) or glass by injecting them with a beam of high energy <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrons" title="Electrons" class="mw-redirect" id="mwpg">electrons</a> from an electron beam accelerator, such as a LINAC (or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_particle_accelerator" title="Linear particle accelerator" id="mwpw">Linac</a>, a type of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_accelerator" title="Particle accelerator" id="mwqA">particle accelerator</a>).<sup about="#mwt35" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-13" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-13"}}"><a href="#cite_note-13" id="mwqQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwqg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwqw">[</span>13<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwrA">]</span></span></a></sup> Inside the Linac, electrons are focused and accelerated to form a beam of high-speed particles. Electrons emerging from the accelerator can have energies up to 25<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwrQ"> </span>MeV and are moving at an appreciable fraction (95 – 99+ percent) of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light" title="Speed of light" id="mwrg">speed of light</a> (<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_relativity" title="Special relativity" id="mwrw">relativistic</a> velocities).</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwsA"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lichtenberg_figure_within_a_acrylic_block.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwsQ"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lichtenberg_figure_within_a_acrylic_block.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Lichtenberg_figure_within_a_acrylic_block.jpg/250px-Lichtenberg_figure_within_a_acrylic_block.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Lichtenberg_figure_within_a_acrylic_block.jpg/500px-Lichtenberg_figure_within_a_acrylic_block.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="3929" data-file-height="5102" data-file-type="bitmap" height="325" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwsg"></a><figcaption id="mwsw">Lichtenberg figure captured in an acrylic block.</figcaption></figure>

<p id="mwtA">If the electron beam is aimed towards a thick acrylic specimen, the electrons easily penetrate the surface of the acrylic, rapidly decelerating as they collide with molecules inside the plastic, finally coming to rest deep inside the specimen. Since acrylic is an excellent electrical insulator, these electrons become temporarily trapped within the specimen, forming a plane of excess negative charge. Positive "mirror" charges are attracted by the building internal negative charge, accumulating on the outer surfaces of the specimen. Under continued irradiation, the amount of trapped charge builds until the effective voltage inside the specimen reaches millions of volts.<sup about="#mwt38" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-14" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-14"}}"><a href="#cite_note-14" id="mwtQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwtg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwtw">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwuA">]</span></span></a></sup> Once the electrical stress exceeds the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dielectric_strength" title="Dielectric strength" id="mwuQ">dielectric strength</a> of the plastic, some portions suddenly become conductive in a process called <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_breakdown#Failure_of_electrical_insulation" title="Electrical breakdown" id="mwug">dielectric breakdown</a>.</p>

<p id="mwuw">During breakdown, branching tree or fern-like conductive channels rapidly form and propagate through the plastic, allowing the trapped charge to suddenly rush out in a miniature <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning" title="Lightning" id="mwvA">lightning</a>-like flash and bang. Breakdown of a charged specimen may also be manually triggered by poking the plastic with a pointed conductive object to create a point of excessive voltage stress. During the discharge, the powerful <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_spark" title="Electric spark" id="mwvQ">electric sparks</a> leave thousands of branching chains of fractures behind, creating a permanent Lichtenberg figure inside the specimen. Although the internal charge within the specimen is negative, the discharge is initiated from the positively charged exterior surfaces of the specimen, so that the resulting discharge creates a positive Lichtenberg figure. These objects are sometimes called <i id="mwvg">electron trees</i>, <i id="mwvw">beam trees</i>, or <i id="mwwA">lightning trees</i>.</p>

<p id="mwwQ">As the electrons rapidly decelerate inside the acrylic, they also generate powerful <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-rays" title="X-rays" class="mw-redirect" id="mwwg">X-rays</a>. Residual electrons and X-rays darken the acrylic by introducing defects (color centers) in a process called <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solarisation_(physics)" title="Solarisation (physics)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwww">solarization</a>. Solarization initially turns acrylic specimens a lime green color, which then changes to an amber color after the specimen has been discharged. The color usually fades over time, and gentle heating, combined with oxygen, accelerates the fading process.<sup about="#mwt41" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-15" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-15"}}"><a href="#cite_note-15" id="mwxA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwxQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwxg">[</span>15<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwxw">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="7" id="mwyA" aria-labelledby="On_wood"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="On_wood">On wood</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Lichtenberg_figure&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: On wood"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt42" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwyQ" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Main article","href":"./Template:Main_article"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Fractal burning"}},"i":0}}]}"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237" about="#mwt43" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" data-mw="{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}"></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt42" id="mwyg">Main article: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractal_burning" title="Fractal burning">Fractal burning</a></div>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwyw"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leopardwood_9_x_24.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwzA"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leopardwood_9_x_24.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Leopardwood_9_x_24.jpg/330px-Leopardwood_9_x_24.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Leopardwood_9_x_24.jpg/960px-Leopardwood_9_x_24.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="3313" data-file-height="1257" data-file-type="bitmap" height="121" width="320" class="mw-file-element" id="mwzQ"></a><figcaption id="mwzg">Lichtenberg branching figure in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopardwood" title="Leopardwood" class="mw-redirect" id="mwzw">leopardwood</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mw0A">Lichtenberg figures can also be produced on wood. The types of wood and grain patterns affect the shape of the Lichtenberg figure produced.<sup about="#mwt47" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-16" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-16"}}"><a href="#cite_note-16" id="mw0Q"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw0g"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw0w">[</span>16<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw1A">]</span></span></a></sup> By applying a coat of electrolytic solution to the surface of the wood, the resistance of the surface drops considerably. Two electrodes are then placed on the wood and a high voltage is passed across them. Current from the electrodes will cause the surface of the wood to heat up until the electrolyte boils and the wooden surface burns. Because the charred surface of the wood is mildly conductive, the surface of the wood will burn in a pattern outwards from the electrodes. Applying fractal burning to wood can be dangerous; it results in deaths every year from <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrocution" title="Electrocution" id="mw1Q">electrocution</a>.<sup about="#mwt50" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-17" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-17"}}"><a href="#cite_note-17" id="mw1g"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw1w"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw2A">[</span>17<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw2Q">]</span></span></a></sup></p>
